author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell makes a chilling argument about how the media treats high profile women, pointing to Caroline Flack and Princess Diana as examples of a pattern he says goes beyond simple bad reporting. He references the documentary The Corporation, which argues that if a corporation were a person, it would be diagnosed as a psychopath, and applies that same idea to how media institutions behave collectively, even when the individual journalists inside them insist they're just seeking truth and justice. The most unsettling part of the argument, the moment someone like Diana dies, the same machine that tore her down instantly flips into mourning her as the nation's princess, turning grief itself into something to consume. A hard hitting, uncomfortable watch about the media's real relationship with the women it covers.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell and his guest dig into a familiar verse, your word is a lamp for my feet, and land on something unexpected, a lamp doesn't light up the whole road ahead, just the ground right in front of you. They connect that limitation directly to the desire for control, something Russell says has shown up throughout his life as both an addict and a famous person, the constant need to know everything's going to be alright further down the path. The conversation lands on a simple but hard truth, you're not in control, you're going to die, and the real invitation is to let go and let the light in one step at a time. A grounded, honest reflection on surrender.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell and his guest reflect on how figures like Princess Diana, Marilyn Monroe, and Grace Kelly captured something almost universal, a kind of appeal that seemingly couldn't be torn down no matter what scandal surrounded them. They argue today's culture is too divisive to ever produce that kind of figure again, pointing to how quickly a modern star can become polarizing the moment they say almost anything. A thoughtful look at what's actually changed, and whether it's the stars themselves or the world around them.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell gets remarkably candid about the lengths his addiction once pushed him to, describing how smuggling drugs concealed on his body between shows became second nature, something he didn't think twice about no matter whose drugs they were. It's a raw, unfiltered look at just how far active addiction can take over someone's judgment and instincts. The clip takes an unexpected turn when a friend reframes even those dark, desperate habits as something that could ultimately serve a purpose now, in his faith and his current life. A genuinely candid moment about where Russell has come from.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell asks a former member of the intelligence community a pointed question, are these institutions fundamentally corrupt, and if the goal was to fix the world, would you get rid of them entirely. Her answer isn't what you'd expect, she argues real democracies actually need intelligence agencies for genuine defense, but only if they stay under proportional democratic control, with real limits on what they're allowed to legally cover up. She closes with a warning about the growing link between big tech and government, calling it one of the most dangerous paths a democracy can go down, something she says Edward Snowden was already warning about a decade ago. A sharp, nuanced take from someone who's actually worked inside these institutions.
